subject: Mathematics

unit.unitOverview: Welcome to Unit 3! In this unit you will learn how to make sense of data – the collections of numbers and facts we meet every single day. When Amina compares the ratings of two books before choosing one, when Hassan looks at the football scores from last weekend, or when Khadija checks how much rain fell each day before the family plants their maize near Garissa, they are all working with data. Averages are the powerful tools that turn a long, confusing list of numbers into one clear, typical value you can actually use.

outcomes: Find the mode – the most common value – and recognise data that is bimodal (has two modes) or has no mode.
Find the median – the middle value when the data is put in order – for both odd and even numbers of values.
Calculate the mean by adding all the values and dividing by how many there are.
Calculate the range – the difference between the highest and lowest values – and use it to describe how consistent data is.
Compare two sets of data using averages and range together.
Choose the most appropriate average for a particular situation and explain your choice.
Think critically about statistics and spot when an average is being used to mislead.

concepts.title: What Is an Average?
concepts.explanation:
An average is a single number that represents what is typical or normal for a whole group of numbers. Instead of trying to hold twenty different scores in your head at once, an average lets you say, “on the whole, this is what the data looks like.” It is like describing a whole class of children with one sensible sentence rather than listing every child separately.

There are three main types of average, and this is the first surprise for many learners: the word “average” does not mean only one thing. The three averages are:

Mode – the value that appears most often (the most popular value).

Median – the middle value when the numbers are placed in order.

Mean – the total of all the values divided by how many values there are.

Each type of average tells us something a little different about the data, and – this is important – for the same set of numbers the three averages can give three different answers. None of them is “wrong”; they simply answer slightly different questions. Part of becoming a skilled mathematician is knowing which question you actually want answered, and then choosing the matching average. We will practise each one carefully in turn, and then learn how to choose between them.
concepts.example: Alongside the averages we will also study the range. The range is not an average – it does not tell us a typical value. Instead it tells us how spread out the data is: are the numbers all bunched close together, or scattered far apart? Knowing both a typical value *and* the spread gives a much fuller picture than either alone. Think of describing the weather in a town: the average temperature tells you what to expect, but the range warns you how much it might swing from day to day.

concepts.title: The Mode – Finding What Is Most Common
concepts.explanation:
The mode is the value that appears most often in a set of data. It is the most popular, most frequent value. To find it you do not need to add or divide anything – you simply count how many times each value appears and pick the one that appears the most.

Look carefully at every value in your data.

Count how many times each different value appears (a frequency table helps).

The value that appears the most times is the mode.

Example 1 – goats brought to market. Over one week, Yusuf records how many goats his family takes to the Burao livestock market each day: 3, 5, 3, 4, 3, 5, 3. The value 3 appears four times, 5 appears twice, and 4 appears once. Since 3 appears most often, the mode is 3 goats.

Example 2 – test marks. A group of marks is 85, 90, 85, 78, 92, 85, 88. Counting: 85 appears three times, and every other mark appears just once. So the mode is 85.

Sometimes two different values are tied for the most appearances. When exactly two values each appear most often, we say the data is bimodal, which means “two modes.” For example, in 2, 3, 3, 5, 7, 7, 9 both the 3 and the 7 appear twice while everything else appears once, so this data is bimodal with modes 3 and 7. And if *every* value appears the same number of times – as in 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, where each appears once – then there is no mode at all.
concepts.example: When is the mode most useful? The mode is the only average that works with categories as well as numbers, because you can find the most common colour, size or type even when there is nothing to add up. It is the perfect average when you want to know the most popular choice. Imagine Halima runs a clothing stall in Eastleigh and sells shirts in sizes 1 to 5. This week she sold sizes: 5, 2, 4, 2, 3, 2, 1, 2, 5, 4, 5. Size 2 was sold four times – more than any other – so the mode is size 2. That tells Halima she should stock more size 2 shirts next week. Here the mean would be almost useless: “the average size sold was 3.2” does not help her order stock, because you cannot buy a shirt of size 3.2!

concepts.title: The Median – Finding the Middle Value
concepts.explanation:
The median is the middle value when all of the data has been arranged in order from smallest to largest. The single most important rule of the median is this: you must put the data in order first. If you try to find the middle of an unordered list, you will almost always get the wrong answer. Ordering first is a habit you must never skip.

Finding the median when there is an odd number of values. Here the method is simple:

Arrange all the values in order from smallest to largest.

Find the single value that sits exactly in the middle.

Example 1 – ages of children. The ages of five children in a Qur’an class are 5, 7, 6, 8, 6. First put them in order: 5, 6, 6, 7, 8. With five values, the middle one is the third value, which is 6. So the median age is 6.

Finding the median when there is an even number of values. When there is an even number of values there is no single number in the middle – instead there are two middle values. To find the median you find the number exactly halfway between them: add the two middle values together and divide by 2.

Add them together and divide by 2 – that is the median.

Example 2 – heights in centimetres. Six children have heights 138, 142, 136, 141, 140, 137 cm. In order: 136, 137, 138, 140, 141, 142. The two middle values are 138 and 140. Halfway between them is (138 + 140) ÷ 2 = 278 ÷ 2 = 139 cm. So the median height is 139 cm. Notice that the median does not even have to be one of the numbers in the list – 139 was not measured, but it is exactly in the middle.

Example 3 – a small even set. For 1, 4, 5, 7, 8, 9 the two middle values are 5 and 7, so the median is (5 + 7) ÷ 2 = 6.
concepts.example: When is the median most useful? The median shines when the data contains a few extreme values (called outliers) that would drag the mean up or down and give a misleading picture. Because the median only cares about the *position* in the middle, one enormous value at the end barely affects it. That is why house prices and incomes are almost always reported using the median: a few very expensive mansions would pull the mean far above what a typical family actually pays. The median answers the question, “what is the value in the very middle, with half above and half below?”

concepts.title: The Mean – Sharing Out Equally
concepts.explanation:
The mean is what most people are thinking of when they say the word “average.” It is the total of all the values divided by how many values there are. A good way to picture the mean is fair sharing: if you gathered up everything and shared it out so that every share was equal, the size of one equal share is the mean.

Here is the three-step method – add, count, divide:

Add up all the values to get the total.

Divide the total by the count. The answer is the mean.

Step-by-step example – measuring heights. Ibrahim wants to compare his height to other children his age, so he measures six friends: 138 cm, 140 cm, 136 cm, 141 cm, 142 cm, 137 cm.

Step 1 – add all the heights: 138 + 140 + 136 + 141 + 142 + 137 = 834 cm.

Step 2 – count the values: there are 6 heights.

Step 3 – divide the total by the count: 834 ÷ 6 = 139. So the mean height is 139 cm.

More examples. For the marks 5, 6, 7 the mean is (5 + 6 + 7) ÷ 3 = 18 ÷ 3 = 6. For Amina’s daily reading times 10, 8, 12, 10, 10 minutes, the mean is (10 + 8 + 12 + 10 + 10) ÷ 5 = 50 ÷ 5 = 10 minutes.

There is a very useful idea hidden inside the mean method. Because mean × count = total, you can work backwards. Suppose the mean of 5 numbers is 24. Then the total of all five numbers must be 5 × 24 = 120. If four of the numbers are 20, 22, 26 and 28, they add to 96, so the fifth number must be 120 − 96 = 24. Being able to move between the mean and the total in either direction is a powerful problem-solving tool that appears again and again.
concepts.example: When is the mean most useful? The mean is the best choice when the values are reasonably similar with no wild outliers, and when you want to take account of every value – for example, comparing the total performance of two teams, or working out a fair share. Its one weakness is exactly the outlier problem: because the mean uses every value, a single very large or very small value can pull it a long way from what is typical. That is a weakness we will return to when we learn to choose the right average.

concepts.title: The Range – Measuring the Spread
concepts.explanation:
The range is not an average. Instead of telling us a typical value, it tells us how spread out the data is – how far apart the biggest and smallest values are. The range is the difference between the highest and lowest values. To find it:

Example 1 – daily temperatures. Over five days near Kismaayo the midday temperatures were 15°C, 19°C, 23°C, 19°C, 16°C. The highest is 23°C and the lowest is 15°C, so the range is 23 − 15 = 8°C.

Example 2 – consistency in practice. Two girls record their daily football-practice times in minutes. Sahra’s times are 10, 8, 2, 10, 20 – highest 20, lowest 2, so her range is 20 − 2 = 18 minutes. Hani’s times are 10, 8, 12, 10, 10 – highest 12, lowest 8, so her range is 12 − 8 = 4 minutes. Hani has a much smaller range, which means she is far more consistent: her practice times barely change from day to day, while Sahra’s swing wildly.

This is the key idea the range gives us:

A small range means the values are close together – the data is consistent and predictable.
concepts.example: A large range means the values are spread far apart – the data is variable and less predictable.

concepts.title: Comparing Data and Choosing the Right Average
concepts.explanation:
Now we bring everything together. When two sets of data are compared, looking at an average and the range together often reveals things that neither shows alone.

Example – two footballers. Two players each score in six matches. Player A scores 12, 12, 13, 13, 14, 14 goals across a season’s games (mean of about 13). Player B scores 8, 10, 13, 14, 16, 19 (also a mean of about 13). Their means are the same, so on paper they look equal. But Player A’s range is 14 − 12 = 2, while Player B’s range is 19 − 8 = 11. Player A is far more consistent; Player B is more unpredictable, brilliant some weeks and quiet others. A coach who wants a reliable scorer every week might choose Player A. The averages alone hid this completely – only the range revealed it.

So which average should you use? Different situations call for different averages. Here is a clear guide:

Use the mode when you want the most popular item, when you are working with categories (colours, sizes, types), or when deciding what to stock or prepare most of.

Use the median when you want the middle value, especially when the data has outliers or extreme values that would distort the mean.

Use the mean when the values are fairly similar with no big outliers, and when you want to take account of every value – for example, comparing totals or working out a fair share.
concepts.example: A worked comparison – salaries at a small business. A shop in Mogadishu pays these monthly wages: the manager earns 60,000 shillings, and three workers earn 35,000, 32,000 and 38,000 shillings. The mean wage is (60,000 + 35,000 + 32,000 + 38,000) ÷ 4 = 165,000 ÷ 4 = 41,250 shillings. But look: three of the four workers earn *less* than that! The manager’s large wage has pulled the mean upward, so the mean gives a misleadingly rosy picture. The median wage – order them 32,000, 35,000, 38,000, 60,000 and average the middle two – is (35,000 + 38,000) ÷ 2 = 36,500 shillings, which is much closer to what most workers actually earn. When there is an outlier like the manager’s wage, the median is usually the fairer, more honest choice.

methods.title: How to find the mean
steps: Add up all the values to get the total.
Count how many values there are.
Divide the total by the count.
Check the answer lies between the lowest and highest values.

methods.title: How to find the median
steps: Write the values in order from smallest to largest.
If the count is odd, pick the single middle value.
If the count is even, average the two middle values.

methods.title: How to choose the right average
methods.example: A shop's sales for six normal days are 40, 42, 41, 43, 39, 40 loaves, but one exceptional festival day sold 95 loaves. Which average best describes a typical day's sales?
steps: For the most popular item or a category, use the mode.
If there is an outlier or extreme value, use the median.
If the values are similar and you want every value counted, use the mean.

methods.title: Median of an even set
methods.example: A basketball player scores 14, 18, 22, 16, 20, 16 in six games. Find the mode, median and mean.
steps: Mode: 16 appears twice, more than any other, so the mode is 16.
Median: order them — 14, 16, 16, 18, 20, 22.
With six values the two middle ones are the 3rd and 4th: 16 and 18.

methods.title: Find and use the range
methods.example: Two archers score: Archer A — 7, 8, 7, 8, 7, 8, 7; Archer B — 4, 9, 6, 10, 5, 11, 6. Find each mean and range, and say who is more consistent.
steps: Archer A total = 52, mean = 52 ÷ 7 ≈ 7.4; range = 8 − 7 = 1.
Archer B total = 51, mean = 51 ÷ 7 ≈ 7.3; range = 11 − 4 = 7.
Their means are almost the same, but Archer A’s range is far smaller, so Archer A is much more consistent.

methods.title: Work backwards from the mean
methods.example: The mean of 5 numbers is 24. Four of them are 20, 22, 26 and 28. Find the fifth.
steps: Total needed = mean × count = 24 × 5 = 120.
The four known numbers add to 20 + 22 + 26 + 28 = 96.
So the fifth number = 120 − 96 = 24.

workedExamples.title: Find the mode
workedExamples.solution: Count each value. 5 appears three times, 8 appears twice, 12 and 10 appear once each. The value appearing most often is 5, so the mode is 5.

workedExamples.title: Find the median of an odd set
workedExamples.solution: First order the data: 8, 11, 12, 15, 16, 19, 23. There are 7 values, so the middle one is the 4th value, which is 15. The median is 15.

workedExamples.title: Find the mean
workedExamples.solution: Add: 6 + 9 + 12 + 15 + 18 = 60. Count: there are 5 values. Divide: 60 ÷ 5 = 12. The mean is 12. (Check: 12 lies between the lowest, 6, and the highest, 18 — sensible.)

workedExamples.title: Median of an even set
workedExamples.prompt: A basketball player scores 14, 18, 22, 16, 20, 16 in six games. Find the mode, median and mean.
workedExamples.solution: Mode: 16 appears twice, more than any other, so the mode is 16. Median: order them — 14, 16, 16, 18, 20, 22. With six values the two middle ones are the 3rd and 4th: 16 and 18. Median = (16 + 18) ÷ 2 = 17. Mean: total = 14+18+22+16+20+16 = 106; 106 ÷ 6 = 17.7 (to one decimal place).

workedExamples.title: Find and use the range
workedExamples.prompt: Two archers score: Archer A — 7, 8, 7, 8, 7, 8, 7; Archer B — 4, 9, 6, 10, 5, 11, 6. Find each mean and range, and say who is more consistent.
workedExamples.solution: Archer A total = 52, mean = 52 ÷ 7 ≈ 7.4; range = 8 − 7 = 1. Archer B total = 51, mean = 51 ÷ 7 ≈ 7.3; range = 11 − 4 = 7. Their means are almost the same, but Archer A’s range is far smaller, so Archer A is much more consistent.

workedExamples.title: Work backwards from the mean
workedExamples.prompt: The mean of 5 numbers is 24. Four of them are 20, 22, 26 and 28. Find the fifth.
workedExamples.solution: Total needed = mean × count = 24 × 5 = 120. The four known numbers add to 20 + 22 + 26 + 28 = 96. So the fifth number = 120 − 96 = 24.

workedExamples.title: Choose the right average
workedExamples.prompt: A data set is 5, 7, 8, 8, 9, 25. Find the mode, median and mean, and decide which best represents a typical value.
workedExamples.solution: Mode = 8 (appears twice). Median: already ordered, two middle values are 8 and 8, so median = 8. Mean: total = 62, 62 ÷ 6 ≈ 10.3. The value 25 is an outlier that has pulled the mean up to 10.3, well above most of the data. So the median (or mode), 8, best represents the typical value here, because the mean is distorted by the outlier.

workedExamples.title: Compare with mean and range
workedExamples.prompt: Two classes take the same test. Class A: mean 78, range 15. Class B: mean 78, range 35. Which class was more consistent, and which might have more pupils needing extra help?
workedExamples.solution: Both classes have the same mean, so on average they did equally well. But Class A has the smaller range (15), so it was more consistent — pupils scored close together. Class B’s larger range (35) means scores were more spread out, so Class B is more likely to have some pupils who scored very low and need extra help.

activities.title: Family Data Detective
activities.materials: paper, a pencil, and your family members.
steps: Choose something to measure: the ages, heights, or shoe sizes of everyone in your household.
Write down every value in a neat list.
Find the mode, the median, the mean and the range of your data.
Talk about it: which average best describes your family? Is anyone an outlier?
Keep your results – you can compare them with a friend’s family and see whose data is more spread out.

activities.title: The Weather Tracker Investigation
activities.materials: a way to note the temperature (a thermometer, a phone, or a weather report) and a notebook.
steps: For one whole week, record the midday temperature each day.
At the end of the week, find the mean temperature and the range.
Was the week warm or cool overall (mean)? Was it steady or changeable (range)?
Predict next week’s pattern, then track it and see how close you were.

activities.title: The Dice Mean Game
activities.materials: one or two dice (or numbers 1–6 written on folded paper to draw from).
steps: Each player rolls the dice five times and writes down the five numbers.
Everyone calculates the mean of their own five rolls.
The player with the highest mean wins the round.
Play several rounds. Does anyone’s mean stay close to 3.5 – the mean you expect from a fair die?
This game shows how the mean settles near a predictable value the more you play.

activities.title: Market Stall Stock Planner (Mode in Action)
activities.materials: paper and pencil, and your imagination as a shopkeeper.
steps: Pretend you run a sambusa stall. Over ten days you sell these numbers of trays: 3, 5, 4, 5, 6, 5, 4, 5, 7, 5.
Find the mode – the number of trays you sell most often.
Use the mode to decide how many trays to prepare on a typical day. Why is the mode better than the mean here?

activities.title: The Misleading Statistic Challenge (Family or Group Task)

rules.title: Order the data before finding the median
rules.text: The median is the middle value when all of the data has been arranged in order from smallest to largest. You must always sort the data first – finding the middle of an unordered list almost always gives the wrong answer.

rules.title: Count occurrences to find the mode
rules.text: The mode is the value that appears most often. Count how many times each value appears (a frequency table helps) and pick the value with the highest count. A data set can have no mode, one mode, or be bimodal with two modes.

rules.title: Add, count, then divide for the mean
rules.text: The mean is the total of all the values divided by how many values there are. Add every value to get the total, count how many values there are, then divide the total by the count.

rules.title: Subtract to find the range
rules.text: The range is the difference between the highest and the lowest value in a data set. It measures how spread out the data is, not a typical value – a small range means the data is more consistent.

rules.title: Choose the average that suits the situation
rules.text: Use the mode for the most popular category, the median when there is an outlier or extreme value, and the mean when the values are similar and every value should count equally.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain the key idea in The Range – Measuring the Spread.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: The range is not an average. Instead of telling us a typical value, it tells us how spread out the data is – how far apart the biggest and smallest values are. The range is the difference between the highest and lowest values. To find it: Example 1 – daily temperatures. Over five days near Kismaayo the midday temperatures were 15°C, 19°C, 23°C, 19°C, 16°C. reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain the key idea in Comparing Data and Choosing the Right Average.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer:
Now we bring everything together. When two sets of data are compared, looking at an average and the range together often reveals things that neither shows alone.

Example – two footballers. Two players each score in six matches. Player A scores 12, 12, 13, 13, 14, 14 goals across a season’s games (mean of about 13). Player B scores 8, 10, 13, 14, 16, 19 (also a mean of about 13). Their means are the same, so on paper they look equal. But Player A’s range is 14 − 12 = 2, while Player B’s range is 19 − 8 = 11. Player A is far more consistent; Player B is more unpredictable, brilliant some weeks and quiet others. A coach who wants a reliable scorer every week might choose Player A. The averages alone hid this completely – only the range revealed it.
